introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

The paper contains eight questions.
enonce_intro_markdown: A particle $P$, of mass $m$, is projected vertically upwards from a point $O$ with speed $\dfrac{2g}{k}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in a medium whose resistance to motion is of magnitude $kv$ per unit mass, where $v$ is the speed of $P$ and $k$ is a positive constant.

questions.corrige_markdown:
Measure the displacement $x$ upwards from $O$. While the particle moves upwards, $v$ is its (positive) speed and its acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

Per unit mass, two forces act on $P$, and both point downwards (against the upward motion): the weight $g$ and the resistance $kv$. Newton's second law (per unit mass), taking upwards as positive, gives

$$v\frac{dv}{dx} = -g - kv. \qquad\blacksquare$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
The particle $P$ attains the highest point $H$ of its path. Show further that
$$OH = \frac{g}{k^2}(2-\ln 3)\ \text{metres.}$$

*[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
From the equation of motion, $\dfrac{v\,dv}{g+kv} = -dx$. At $O$, $x=0$ and $v=\dfrac{2g}{k}$; at the highest point $H$, $x = OH$ and $v = 0$. Integrating between these limits:

$$OH = \int_{v=2g/k}^{0} \frac{-v}{g+kv}\,dv = \int_{0}^{2g/k}\frac{v}{g+kv}\,dv.$$

Write the integrand as
$$\frac{v}{g+kv} = \frac1k\cdot\frac{(g+kv)-g}{g+kv} = \frac1k\left(1-\frac{g}{g+kv}\right).$$

Hence
$$OH = \frac1k\left[\,v - \frac{g}{k}\ln(g+kv)\right]_{0}^{2g/k}
= \frac1k\left[\frac{2g}{k} - \frac{g}{k}\ln(g+2g) + \frac{g}{k}\ln g\right]
= \frac1k\cdot\frac{g}{k}\left(2-\ln\frac{3g}{g}\right).$$

$$\boxed{\,OH = \frac{g}{k^2}\,(2-\ln 3)\ \text{metres}\,}$$

(Numerically $2-\ln 3 \approx 0.9014 > 0$, as it must be.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that the particle $P$ reaches another point $M$ with speed $\dfrac{g}{2k}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ as it traces its path back to $O$, the point of projection, prove that
$$HM = \frac{g}{k^2}\left(\ln 2 - \frac12\right).$$

*[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the way down the resistance acts upwards, against the motion. Measure the distance $s$ downwards from $H$, starting from rest. Per unit mass the weight $g$ acts downwards and the resistance $kv$ upwards, so

$$v\frac{dv}{ds} = g - kv \quad\Longrightarrow\quad ds = \frac{v\,dv}{g-kv}.$$

At $H$, $s=0$ and $v=0$; at $M$, $s = HM$ and $v = \dfrac{g}{2k}$ (this is less than the terminal speed $g/k$, so $g-kv>0$ throughout). Therefore

$$HM = \int_0^{g/2k}\frac{v}{g-kv}\,dv.$$

Write
$$\frac{v}{g-kv} = -\frac1k + \frac{g}{k}\cdot\frac{1}{g-kv}$$
(check: $\dfrac{-(g-kv)+g}{k(g-kv)} = \dfrac{kv}{k(g-kv)}$). Then

$$HM = \left[-\frac{v}{k} - \frac{g}{k^2}\ln(g-kv)\right]_0^{g/2k}
= -\frac{g}{2k^2} - \frac{g}{k^2}\ln\frac{g/2}{g}
= -\frac{g}{2k^2} + \frac{g}{k^2}\ln 2.$$

$$\boxed{\,HM = \frac{g}{k^2}\left(\ln 2 - \frac12\right)\,}\qquad\blacksquare$$

(Numerically $\ln 2 - \tfrac12 \approx 0.1931>0$, and it is smaller than $OH$'s factor $0.9014$, as expected: $M$ lies between $H$ and $O$.)
